title: A diabetes follow-up gap
stem: A client with diabetes has normal vision and asks whether a recent visual-acuity check replaces retinal screening. Which explanation is most accurate?
options: Retinal screening can detect damage before vision changes
Screening can wait until blurred vision develops
A normal visual-acuity check rules out retinal disease
Glucose readings in range make retinal screening unnecessary
why: Retinal disease may develop before the client notices a vision problem.
Waiting for visual symptoms may delay detection and treatment.
Visual acuity does not establish that the retinal blood vessels are healthy.
Glucose management reduces risk but does not replace the recommended eye assessment.
takeaway: Explain the preventive purpose of diabetes eye screening.
learningObjective: Explain the preventive purpose of diabetes eye screening.

title: Assessing a written action plan
stem: A client correctly demonstrates asthma inhaler technique and routine dosing but cannot identify when the written action plan says to seek urgent help. What should the nurse do next?
options: Review routine inhaler technique with the client
Practise worsening-symptom decisions using the action plan
Explain the written action plan a second time
Arrange a follow-up teaching call next week
why: Technique is already demonstrated and is not the identified learning gap.
Scenario decisions let the nurse teach and verify the missing escalation skill now.
Another explanation may help, but it does not establish that the client can apply the instructions.
A later call does not resolve the current inability to recognize when urgent help is needed.
takeaway: Evaluate whether clients can apply action-plan escalation instructions.
learningObjective: Evaluate whether clients can apply action-plan escalation instructions.

title: A symptom diary with purpose
stem: A client with recurrent headaches is preparing a diary to help identify episode patterns and treatment response. Which entry is most useful?
options: Headache was severe; checked blood pressure, ate dinner, and stayed home rather than visiting family.
Headache began Monday afternoon; missed work, cancelled shopping, and felt worried about another painful week.
Pain began 14:00 after missed lunch; nausea; prescribed medicine at 14:15; pain eased by 15:00.
Headache improved by evening; mother also has headaches; my last eye examination was two months ago.
why: The entry describes impact but lacks episode timing and treatment response needed for the stated goal.
Timing and impact are useful, but the entry does not connect triggers, accompanying symptoms or treatment response.
This entry links timing, a possible trigger, an associated symptom and response to treatment.
Background history is useful in assessment but does not adequately describe this episode or what improved it.
takeaway: Record symptom context and response when preparing for clinical review.
learningObjective: Record symptom context and response when preparing for clinical review.

title: Weight monitoring in an action plan
stem: A client with heart failure has a daily weight-reporting plan but compares readings taken in different clothing before and after meals. Which routine should the nurse recommend?
options: Weigh every Sunday before breakfast in similar clothing
Average morning and evening readings taken around meals
Weigh each evening after dinner in usual daytime clothes
Weigh each morning before breakfast using consistent conditions
why: Weekly measurements may miss changes the prescribed daily plan is intended to identify.
Food, fluid and clothing differences can obscure interpretation of an averaged trend.
Evening food and fluid intake can vary; morning conditions provide a more reproducible baseline.
Morning measurement after voiding, with the same scale and similar clothing, supports comparison within the reporting plan.
takeaway: Standardize home measurements used to guide follow-up.
learningObjective: Standardize home measurements used to guide follow-up.

title: Planning ongoing self-management
stem: A client with a chronic-condition action plan has a working telephone but no internet. The clinic has a daytime nurse line and an after-hours advice service. Which arrangements make the plan usable? Select all that apply.
options: Send symptom alerts through the clinic patient portal
Write the daytime and after-hours telephone routes on the plan
Leave worsening symptoms on the routine booking voicemail
Practise which symptom changes require each contact route
why: The client cannot access the portal, so this route cannot support the home plan.
Available telephone routes provide a practical way to obtain advice at different times.
A booking voicemail may not provide timely clinical triage for worsening symptoms.
Practising specific trigger-and-contact decisions verifies that the written plan can guide action.
takeaway: Link self-monitoring findings to feasible action and contact instructions.
learningObjective: Link self-monitoring findings to feasible action and contact instructions.

title: Exercise confidence after rehabilitation
stem: A client is clinically ready to continue rehabilitation exercises at home and performs them correctly. They worry about deciding what to do if warning symptoms occur while alone. What is most useful?
options: Extend the supervised exercise visits for another week
Rehearse the home plan using a warning-symptom scenario
Provide another copy of the exercise instruction sheet
Refer the client to a community exercise group
why: Further supervision may provide reassurance but does not directly test the decision the client fears making alone.
Rehearsal addresses the specific transition skill and allows correction before independent practice.
Exercise instructions do not necessarily resolve uncertainty about symptom escalation.
A group may support maintenance later, but the client still needs a usable response to symptoms.
takeaway: Prepare clients to apply rehabilitation learning outside supervised settings.
learningObjective: Prepare clients to apply rehabilitation learning outside supervised settings.

title: A dietary goal and cultural foods
stem: A client with hypertension wants to retain a family stew that uses several stock cubes. They can read food labels and ask for a practical sodium-reduction change. Which approach best fits?
options: Reduce the serving size of the usual stew
Give a standard weekly low-sodium meal plan
Try lower-sodium stock with familiar herbs and spices
Repeat teaching about locating sodium on labels
why: A smaller serving may reduce sodium but may also reduce the meal amount rather than address its concentrated sodium source.
A generic plan may be less useful than adapting the meal the client wants to continue.
An acceptable stock substitution targets the identified source while retaining familiar food practices.
The client already reads labels; the immediate request is for a usable recipe change.
takeaway: Adapt health goals within meaningful cultural food practices.
learningObjective: Adapt health goals within meaningful cultural food practices.

title: Financial barriers to prescribed care
stem: A client understands that laboratory monitoring is due this week but missed testing because bus fare was unaffordable. A funded transport service has openings before the test deadline. What should the nurse prioritize?
options: Help the client arrange the available funded transport
Rebook at the same laboratory for next month
Review how the laboratory results guide treatment
Ask the prescriber whether monitoring can be reduced
why: This directly addresses the known barrier while preserving the planned monitoring interval.
A later booking may delay needed monitoring and leaves the cost barrier unresolved.
Understanding is already present; more education does not supply transport.
Clinical changes can be reviewed when needed, but an available access solution can preserve the existing plan.
takeaway: Address access barriers to recommended preventive monitoring.
learningObjective: Address access barriers to recommended preventive monitoring.

title: Chronic pain and valued activity
stem: A client with an established chronic-pain plan alternates doing all housework on good days and remaining inactive afterward. Which teaching is most relevant?
options: Finish as much as possible whenever pain is low
Stop all housework until pain resolves
Use pain alone to decide every day's workload
Plan manageable activity periods and breaks across days
why: Overactivity may contribute to the reported flare-and-rest cycle.
Complete avoidance can reduce function and participation.
Pain fluctuates and may not support consistent pacing alone.
Pacing supports steadier participation within an individualized plan.
takeaway: Use activity pacing to support sustainable function with chronic pain.
learningObjective: Use activity pacing to support sustainable function with chronic pain.

title: Diabetes appointment preparation
stem: A client has variable glucose readings and sometimes delays refills because of cost. Which preparations would help the diabetes team assess the current plan? Select all that apply.
options: Bring meter records with symptoms and meal timing
Submit the weekly glucose average as the glucose record
Describe when cost led to delayed refills
Use the previous visit medication list for reconciliation
why: Timed readings and symptoms help the team interpret variability and safety.
An average can conceal clinically relevant highs, lows and timing patterns.
Actual access-related interruptions may explain variability and identify a support need.
A previous list may not reflect current use, changes or added products; current treatment needs review.
takeaway: Prepare complete clinically relevant information for chronic-disease review.
learningObjective: Prepare complete clinically relevant information for chronic-disease review.

title: Food insecurity screening
stem: A client with a stable weight says, "We have food today, but it often runs out before payday." What should the nurse do next?
options: Explore how often food runs out and discuss available support
Calculate current energy needs from the stable weight
Review the nutrient balance of yesterday's meals
Schedule a weight check at the next routine visit
why: The recurring access problem needs further screening and a client-led discussion of practical resources.
Energy estimates do not establish whether the client can reliably obtain food.
Meal quality matters, but one day does not describe the recurring shortage.
Waiting for weight change can miss an existing material barrier even when weight is stable.
takeaway: Recognize unreliable food access even when food is available today.
learningObjective: Recognize unreliable food access even when food is available today.

title: Housing and asthma prevention
stem: A parent demonstrates correct asthma treatment and keeps a trigger diary. Building leaks repeatedly leave the rented home damp and mould returns after cleaning. What best complements the child's care?
options: Repeat the inhaler-technique teaching session
Connect the family with housing and environmental-health resources
Provide another household surface-cleaning checklist
Ask the parent to extend the trigger diary
why: Technique is already correct and does not remedy recurring building dampness.
Structural moisture problems may require resources beyond household self-care.
Cleaning alone is unlikely to resolve mould when the moisture source persists.
Further tracking may document exposure but does not address the established housing barrier.
takeaway: Address housing conditions that obstruct chronic-disease prevention.
learningObjective: Address housing conditions that obstruct chronic-disease prevention.

title: Designing a community program
stem: A nurse plans a neighbourhood nutrition program. Residents' priorities, food resources and access barriers have not yet been established. What should occur first?
options: Book a community kitchen near the clinic
Adapt an existing healthy-eating workshop
Consult residents about needs and participation barriers
Recruit facilitators experienced in nutrition teaching
why: A venue decision should reflect who will attend and how they can reach and use it.
Existing content may be useful after local needs are known.
Resident input provides the evidence needed to choose relevant content and feasible delivery.
Facilitator skills should be selected for the priorities and delivery requirements identified.
takeaway: Assess community priorities before designing health-promotion activities.
learningObjective: Assess community priorities before designing health-promotion activities.

title: Screening uptake disparity
stem: A clinic finds lower screening completion among clients who need interpretation, but has not established why appointments are missed. What is the best next step?
options: Add translated reminders to the current booking system
Offer an additional evening screening clinic
Start an outreach telephone reminder campaign
Review booking and interpreter access with affected clients
why: Translated reminders may help if information is the barrier, but that cause has not been established.
Extra hours address scheduling barriers that may or may not explain this disparity.
More calls may preserve existing communication barriers if the process is not accessible.
Client-informed assessment can identify the actual communication or access changes required.
takeaway: Investigate access barriers before explaining screening disparities as preference.
learningObjective: Investigate access barriers before explaining screening disparities as preference.

title: Accessible group education
stem: Residents want a health class, but their bus route ends at 18:00 and several need interpretation. The community room has accessible ground-floor entry. Which arrangements support attendance and participation? Select all that apply.
options: Finish the session before the last return bus
Offer the session at 19:00 to avoid daytime traffic
Arrange the interpretation residents have requested
Use written English handouts as the language support
Hold the session in the accessible community room
why: The end time must allow participants to use their available return transport.
This time falls after the stated transport service ends.
Appropriate interpretation supports meaningful participation in discussion.
English handouts do not address the stated interpretation need.
An accessible local setting removes a physical participation barrier.
takeaway: Match community education arrangements to actual transport, language and physical-access needs.
learningObjective: Match community education arrangements to actual transport, language and physical-access needs.

title: Understanding prevention levels
stem: A community program offers blood-pressure screening to adults without diagnosed hypertension. What is the main prevention purpose?
options: Rehabilitation after established complications
Early identification for assessment and management
Treatment of an acute hypertensive emergency
Confirmation of diagnosis from any single reading
why: Rehabilitation addresses established functional consequences rather than initial detection.
Screening can identify people needing further clinical evaluation.
Routine screening is not acute emergency treatment.
One screening measurement does not automatically establish a diagnosis.
takeaway: Explain screening as early detection requiring appropriate follow-up.
learningObjective: Explain screening as early detection requiring appropriate follow-up.

title: Responding to a high screening reading
stem: An adult has a blood pressure of 156/92 mm Hg at a fair after rushing upstairs. They report no chest pain, dyspnoea or neurological symptoms. What should the nurse do next?
options: Arrange routine follow-up using the first reading
Begin teaching a week-long home monitoring schedule
Repeat the measurement after appropriate seated rest
Record the elevation as a temporary exertional effect
why: Follow-up may be needed, but a properly repeated reading should first improve the quality of the screening information.
Home monitoring may assist later evaluation; it does not replace correcting the current measurement conditions.
Standardized rest and positioning help determine whether the initial result persists and guide subsequent follow-up.
Recent activity can affect the result but cannot establish that the elevation is harmless.
takeaway: Confirm screening measurements under suitable conditions and arrange appropriate follow-up.
learningObjective: Confirm screening measurements under suitable conditions and arrange appropriate follow-up.

title: Following up a referral
stem: A client with hearing loss has not contacted a smoking-cessation service because telephone speech is difficult. They use text comfortably, and the service accepts online text referrals. What is best?
options: Help complete the text referral with the client's agreement
Rehearse a telephone conversation with the client
Provide the service's printed self-help information
Arrange a telephone callback at a quieter time
why: The available text route matches the demonstrated communication ability and can connect the client to the intended service.
Practice does not necessarily overcome the hearing-related access barrier.
Written advice may be useful but does not establish the requested service connection.
A quieter time may not make telephone speech accessible for this client.
takeaway: Verify whether referral pathways are usable for the client.
learningObjective: Verify whether referral pathways are usable for the client.

title: Choosing a program outcome
stem: A prenatal class aims to help participants choose what to do when warning symptoms develop. Which outcome best evaluates that objective?
options: Confidence ratings about coping with pregnancy symptoms
Recall scores for a list of pregnancy warning signs
Completion rates for written clinic contact information
Accuracy of action choices in realistic symptom scenarios
why: Confidence is meaningful but may not match correct decisions.
Recall of signs does not establish which action the participant would take.
Having contact information is useful but does not test recognition and escalation.
Scenario decisions directly measure the intended ability to select an appropriate response.
takeaway: Match program evaluation to the intended learning outcome.
learningObjective: Match program evaluation to the intended learning outcome.

title: Community partnership
stem: An Indigenous community invites a clinic to help plan a wellness program and asks that local priorities guide it. Which actions support this partnership? Select all that apply.
options: Ask the community to choose who participates in planning
Use locally identified priorities and knowledge in the design
Adopt the schedule and content of another community's successful program
Invite participants to describe whether the program feels culturally safe
why: Community-selected participation supports self-determination and relevant planning.
Local knowledge and priorities should shape a program developed in partnership.
Success elsewhere does not establish that its schedule and content fit this community; local selection and adaptation are needed.
Participants' experiences provide evidence about cultural safety that provider intentions cannot establish.
takeaway: Build wellness programs with community-defined participation and priorities.
learningObjective: Build wellness programs with community-defined participation and priorities.

title: A culturally meaningful health goal
stem: An Indigenous client wants traditional healing included in a diabetes plan. The nurse has not yet explored what the client wants included. What should the nurse do first?
options: Ask which healing practices and supports the client prefers
Request a pharmacist review of possible product interactions
Offer to arrange a meeting with an Elder
Invite family to a diabetes planning appointment
why: The client should define the requested practices and involvement before the nurse selects referrals or coordination.
An interaction review may be relevant if products are involved, but that has not been established.
An Elder may be a desired support, but the nurse should first ask rather than infer that preference.
Family involvement should reflect the client's wishes and may not be the requested support.
takeaway: Ask how clients want traditional healing included in their care.
learningObjective: Ask how clients want traditional healing included in their care.

title: A heat-risk plan
stem: A heat warning predicts several hot days. An older adult lives alone in an apartment that stayed hot overnight during the last warning. They have no symptoms and cannot reach the cooling centre independently. What is the priority preparation?
options: Arrange telephone temperature checks each afternoon
Arrange an accessible ride to a cooled location
Open the apartment windows through the afternoon
Purchase a fan to use in the hottest room
why: Checks may identify concern but do not supply cooling when the home retains heat.
A usable route to cooling addresses the known exposure and mobility barrier before illness develops.
Opening windows when outdoor air is hotter may not cool the apartment.
A fan may improve comfort, but cannot reliably replace access to a cooler location during severe indoor heat.
takeaway: Plan cooling access and social check-ins before heat illness develops.
learningObjective: Plan cooling access and social check-ins before heat illness develops.

title: Air-quality and activity planning
stem: A client with chronic respiratory disease wants to continue outdoor walking during poor air quality. What should the nurse suggest?
options: Keep the usual outdoor route while reducing total walking time
Shorten exposure by completing the route at a faster pace
Use air-quality advice and the action plan to adapt the walk
Suspend exercise until outdoor air quality remains normal for several weeks
why: A shorter outdoor route may still be unsuitable for current air quality and individual risk.
Faster exertion may increase inhaled pollutants despite less time outdoors.
Combining exposure information and the individual plan supports a safer activity choice.
An extended stop may be unnecessary when safer indoor or timing alternatives exist.
takeaway: Adapt activity to environmental conditions and individual respiratory risk.
learningObjective: Adapt activity to environmental conditions and individual respiratory risk.

title: Noise exposure and hearing
stem: A worker reports recurrent ringing after machinery shifts and removes uncomfortable hearing protection intermittently. The next annual hearing test is months away. What is the best advice?
options: Change to a different earplug brand for the next shift
Ask the supervisor for quieter duties when ringing develops
Keep the next annual hearing-test appointment
Seek hearing review and a suitable protection fitting now
why: A different product may help, but unassessed fit and ongoing symptoms need a coordinated review.
Reducing exposure is useful, but waiting for ringing does not ensure protection during the rest of the shift.
The current symptoms and inconsistent protection warrant attention before the routine test date.
Prompt review addresses possible hearing change and the practical reason protection is not used consistently.
takeaway: Respond to noise-related symptoms with assessment and reliable exposure protection.
learningObjective: Respond to noise-related symptoms with assessment and reliable exposure protection.

title: Preparing for medication storage away from home
stem: A pharmacist confirms that a travel medication must stay between 2°C and 8°C and must not freeze. The client has a six-hour journey followed by a hotel stay. Which preparations are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Use transport packaging verified to maintain the stated range
Keep the medication directly against frozen ice packs
Confirm suitable monitored storage at the destination
Use the hotel minibar at its coldest setting
Keep the original medication identification with the supply
why: Product-matched transport packaging addresses the length and temperature requirements of the journey.
Direct frozen-pack contact can freeze the medication despite the cooler air remaining within range.
Destination storage also needs to meet the actual range rather than relying on a refrigerator label.
An unverified coldest setting can place the product outside its required range or freeze it.
Identification supports correct use and product-specific advice during travel.
takeaway: Plan travel storage using the medication's actual requirements.
learningObjective: Plan travel storage using the medication's actual requirements.

title: Responding to a wellness supplement claim
stem: A client taking several prescriptions wants to add a supplement and asks whether a Canadian product licence makes it suitable for them. What should the nurse recommend first?
options: Review its ingredients against the client's current medicines
Choose a licensed product and begin the labelled dose
Separate the supplement from prescriptions by two hours
Ask the retailer which similar product sells most often
why: Individual medicines and health conditions can change risk; a qualified clinician or pharmacist should review compatibility.
Licensing and label directions do not establish compatibility with this person's treatment.
Spacing does not prevent every pharmacological interaction.
Popularity does not establish safety with this client's medication regimen.
takeaway: Review supplements in the context of the client's medications and conditions.
learningObjective: Review supplements in the context of the client's medications and conditions.

title: Making an emergency plan usable
stem: An adult with food allergy demonstrates correct use of prescribed epinephrine auto-injectors. For restaurant meals, the devices stay in the locked car while the client carries emergency contact numbers. Which change best makes the emergency plan usable?
options: Ask restaurant staff to keep the contact card at the desk
Carry the prescribed devices where they are immediately accessible
Choose a restaurant closer to an emergency department
Have a companion check the car location before each meal
why: Contact information is useful but does not provide the prescribed immediate treatment.
Rapid access to the devices is necessary for the client to act on the emergency plan if a reaction occurs.
Proximity to a hospital does not replace access to prescribed rescue treatment at the meal.
Knowing the car location still leaves retrieval as an avoidable delay.
takeaway: Check immediate access to the supplies required by a community emergency plan.
learningObjective: Check immediate access to the supplies required by a community emergency plan.

title: Planning care during fasting
stem: A client taking insulin plans to observe Ramadan in two months and asks how meal-time changes will affect treatment. What should the nurse recommend?
options: Move the current doses to the new meal times
Add glucose checks while retaining the current regimen
Arrange a pre-fast review with the diabetes team
Review the plan after the first week of fasting
why: Dose timing changes may be needed, but timing alone cannot establish a safe individualized regimen.
Monitoring is useful, but it does not replace assessment of fasting risk and possible treatment changes.
A pre-fast review can assess individual risk and agree on medication, monitoring and when to stop fasting or seek help.
Waiting until fasting begins loses the opportunity for planned risk reduction.
takeaway: Coordinate individualized care when fasting changes intake and treatment needs.
learningObjective: Coordinate individualized care when fasting changes intake and treatment needs.

title: Healthy eating with limited cooking facilities
stem: A client in temporary accommodation has a refrigerator and microwave but no stove. They want affordable meals with vegetables and protein and can store two days of food. Which plan is most feasible?
options: Prepare a large stockpot of bean soup for the whole week
Buy a countertop cooker for full-kitchen batch recipes
Use restaurant delivery for the daily vegetable-and-protein meal
Combine canned beans, microwave vegetables and cooked grains
why: The proposed batch requires a stove and exceeds the available storage period.
Buying equipment introduces a cost and may not be allowed or needed in the current accommodation.
Frequent delivery may not meet the client's affordability goal.
These foods can provide the requested meal components with the equipment and storage available.
takeaway: Match food advice to available storage and preparation facilities.
learningObjective: Match food advice to available storage and preparation facilities.

title: Evaluating home-monitoring logs
stem: Which patterns should a nurse discuss with a client who brings a symptom log? Select all that apply.
options: Repeated symptoms linked to a particular activity
Changes after a prescribed intervention
Missing entries as definite proof that symptoms were absent
Consistently worsening function despite similar numeric ratings
why: Activity relationships may help identify triggers and adaptations.
Before-and-after patterns support evaluation of the treatment plan.
Missing data cannot establish absence of symptoms.
Function provides important information beyond a single rating.
takeaway: Interpret self-monitoring data with context, missing information and functional changes.
learningObjective: Interpret self-monitoring data with context, missing information and functional changes.

title: A client declines a preventive test
stem: A capable client has had screening benefits, limitations and questions addressed, demonstrates understanding, and declines the test. What should the nurse do next?
options: Document the decision and explain how to revisit it
Schedule another counselling visit to reconsider the decision
Offer a family meeting to discuss the choice
Book the test provisionally to preserve an appointment
why: The informed decision should be respected while preserving a route to future discussion.
Another counselling visit is not required simply because an informed choice differs from the recommendation.
Family discussion can be offered if desired, but is not needed to validate this capable client's decision.
Provisional booking is inconsistent with the current informed refusal unless the client requests it.
takeaway: Preserve informed choice and future access when screening is declined.
learningObjective: Preserve informed choice and future access when screening is declined.

title: A positive stool screening result
stem: An asymptomatic client has an abnormal fecal immunochemical test (FIT) and wants to repeat it until negative. What should the nurse explain?
options: A later negative FIT cancels the initial finding
The abnormal result needs diagnostic follow-up
This result establishes a colorectal cancer diagnosis
New symptoms should determine when follow-up begins
why: A repeat negative result does not resolve the cause of the initial abnormal screening result.
The recommended diagnostic pathway, generally colonoscopy after assessment, investigates the abnormal result.
An abnormal FIT identifies blood; it does not by itself diagnose cancer.
Diagnostic follow-up can be important before symptoms occur.
takeaway: Follow an abnormal screening result through the recommended diagnostic pathway.
learningObjective: Follow an abnormal screening result through the recommended diagnostic pathway.

title: Prevention after cancer treatment
stem: A client completing cancer treatment has an oncology surveillance plan and is also due for a primary-care diabetes review. They think the oncology visits replace general care. What plan should the nurse support?
options: Bring the diabetes questions to the next surveillance visit
Rebook the diabetes review after oncology follow-up ends
Coordinate the diabetes review with the surveillance plan
Request repeat oncology bloodwork at the primary-care visit
why: Oncology can coordinate concerns, but the surveillance visit may not cover routine diabetes management.
General chronic-care needs continue during cancer surveillance.
Shared responsibilities allow cancer follow-up and the current primary-care need to be addressed.
Duplicating tests does not establish who is responsible for the ongoing diabetes review.
takeaway: Integrate survivorship care with ongoing general health maintenance.
learningObjective: Integrate survivorship care with ongoing general health maintenance.

title: Low confidence with new equipment
stem: A client uses a home blood-pressure monitor correctly but worries about a movement-error message when alone. The device manual provides a specific correction. What is most useful next?
options: Demonstrate another measurement while the client watches
Give the client a highlighted copy of the device manual
Teach a relative to perform the measurements
Have the client practise the error-correction steps
why: Watching a normal measurement does not rehearse the specific difficulty the client expects.
Written instructions are useful, but practice can verify whether the client can apply them.
Family help may be available, but the client has demonstrated the basic skill and wants to manage independently.
Guided practice of the identified device problem supports a usable response and confidence.
takeaway: Strengthen confidence by practising the actual home routine and backup plan.
learningObjective: Strengthen confidence by practising the actual home routine and backup plan.

title: Preventive care during unstable housing
stem: A client without a stable address can use a community centre phone at an agreed afternoon time and visits its drop-in service weekly. They have no internet. Which follow-up arrangements are feasible? Select all that apply.
options: Schedule a confidential call at the agreed centre-phone time
Coordinate follow-up with the weekly drop-in service
Send appointment changes to the patient portal
Mail reminders to the address from the last admission
why: An agreed usable phone time can support contact if confidentiality arrangements are confirmed.
A service the client already accesses offers a practical point for continuity.
The client cannot retrieve portal messages with the stated resources.
The historical address does not establish a current reliable route.
takeaway: Adapt follow-up routes to housing and communication realities.
learningObjective: Adapt follow-up routes to housing and communication realities.

title: Preparing a person with limited stamina
stem: A client must learn two home-care skills and says concentration is best after morning rest; a 30-minute afternoon therapy session leaves them exhausted. Which teaching schedule best fits?
options: Two brief morning practice sessions with a rest between
One combined session immediately after afternoon therapy
One evening review of both skills before sleep
Written preparation during therapy followed by a joint review
why: This uses the identified better-energy period and permits breaks and practice for each skill.
The proposed time follows the activity known to exhaust the client.
An evening session may not use the reported period of better concentration.
Concurrent learning during therapy adds demands and may impair both tasks.
takeaway: Match teaching duration and timing to stamina.
learningObjective: Match teaching duration and timing to stamina.

title: A family member dominates education
stem: A capable adult wants to learn their own care and wants a relative present for support. The relative answers every teaching question. What should the nurse do first?
options: Ask the relative to demonstrate the care sequence first
Redirect questions to the client and agree on the relative's role
Arrange separate teaching sessions for the client and relative
Give both people the same written care instructions
why: This continues centring the relative rather than establishing the client's understanding.
Direct client participation respects the stated goal while retaining the desired support.
Separate sessions may help later, but need not be imposed before clarifying roles together.
Shared material does not correct who participates in the current teaching exchange.
takeaway: Keep the client central when involving family in self-care teaching.
learningObjective: Keep the client central when involving family in self-care teaching.

title: A changed learning need
stem: A client previously managed injections independently but now has reduced vision. They want to continue self-care. What is the best next step?
options: Provide a larger-print copy of the injection instructions
Ask a relative to prepare the injections each morning
Observe current technique to identify needed adaptations
Repeat the original injection teaching demonstration
why: Larger print may help but may not address reading dose markings or performing the task.
Family assistance may be appropriate if desired and needed, but current ability has not been assessed.
Observed performance identifies the actual effects of vision change and guides accessible support.
A general refresher does not establish which steps are now difficult.
takeaway: Reassess self-care competence when functional abilities change.
learningObjective: Reassess self-care competence when functional abilities change.

title: Health goals after disability
stem: A client who uses a wheelchair has good upper-body strength and wants to rejoin friends at a community garden. The site has an accessible path but ground-level plots are difficult to reach. Which plan best supports the goal?
options: Begin a walking-endurance program before returning
Arrange home gardening videos with weekly discussion
Join the garden group's seated planning meetings
Arrange reachable raised-bed tasks at the group garden
why: Walking is not required for participation when the environment can be adapted.
Home learning does not provide the desired shared gardening activity.
Planning meetings support social participation but do not provide the hands-on task the client values.
Reachable growing spaces use existing strengths and accessible routes to support the chosen activity.
takeaway: Define health-promotion outcomes around meaningful participation with disability.
learningObjective: Define health-promotion outcomes around meaningful participation with disability.

title: Checking a home plan's feasibility
stem: A client correctly demonstrates a simple home dressing change. Which findings provide evidence that the plan can be carried out at home? Select all that apply.
options: The client can obtain the required dressing supplies
The client identifies a suitable space for the task
The discharge folder has been signed as received
The dressing handout has the client's current address
why: Available supplies are a practical requirement for carrying out the demonstrated skill.
A suitable working space helps establish that the task fits the home setting.
A receipt signature does not establish the resources required for care.
An accurate address supports administration but does not demonstrate task feasibility.
takeaway: Check resources and setting when evaluating a home-care plan.
learningObjective: Check resources and setting when evaluating a home-care plan.

title: A changing prevention priority
stem: A client's chronic conditions are stable, but food will run out tonight and the home heating has been disconnected during cold weather. Which action should the nurse prioritize?
options: Review the current medication schedule for simplification
Connect the client with urgent food and heating assistance
Revise the weekly exercise targets for indoor activity
Provide lower-cost meal-planning information
why: Medication review can continue, but the immediate material needs threaten the feasibility of care now.
Concrete urgent resource support addresses the current lack of food and safe warmth.
Activity adaptation does not supply food or restore a safe living temperature.
Meal advice cannot solve the absence of food tonight or the heating problem.
takeaway: Reprioritize health promotion when basic living conditions change.
learningObjective: Reprioritize health promotion when basic living conditions change.

title: Relating activity to personal values
stem: A client can walk comfortably for ten minutes, dislikes organized exercise classes, and wants energy to play with grandchildren. Which starting goal best supports engagement?
options: Attend a scheduled fitness class twice each week
Track daily steps and compare weekly totals
Plan brief active play periods with gradual increases
Begin a gym-based resistance program each morning
why: The client has expressed dislike for this format, so it may be harder to sustain.
Step tracking can support monitoring but does not directly establish an enjoyable activity linked to the valued role.
A gradual plan linked to the client's own reason for activity can build from current ability.
Resistance training may offer benefits, but this prescribed setting and schedule do not reflect the stated preference.
takeaway: Connect health behaviours with the client's own valued activities.
learningObjective: Connect health behaviours with the client's own valued activities.

title: Preventive-care reminder consent
stem: A client shares a phone with family and is concerned that lock-screen text reminders could reveal a sensitive screening visit. What should the nurse do before enrolling them in reminders?
options: Agree on a safe contact route and acceptable wording
Use the mobile number already recorded in the chart
Select the clinic's standard generic text template
Offer to send the reminder to the household contact
why: The client should determine whether the route and message content are acceptable with the shared device.
An existing number does not establish consent or safety for this use.
Even a generic template may reveal clinic information or may not match the client's preference.
Another recipient introduces a disclosure question that requires the client's agreement.
takeaway: Confirm safe communication preferences for preventive-care reminders.
learningObjective: Confirm safe communication preferences for preventive-care reminders.

title: Interpreting a health trend
stem: A client's walking goal was to reach the nearby shop with less fatigue. After a month they can do this comfortably, but weight is unchanged. Which evaluation best matches the stated goal?
options: The outcome needs another month of weight measurements
The activity goal requires a higher walking intensity
The next evaluation should focus on calorie intake
The improved walking tolerance demonstrates useful progress
why: Weight trends may have other uses, but are not needed to recognize the stated functional improvement.
A higher intensity is not required to acknowledge a goal already achieved.
Nutrition can be discussed when relevant, but it is not the outcome the client selected here.
The client can now complete the chosen activity with less fatigue, which directly meets the functional aim.
takeaway: Evaluate health behaviour using meaningful functional outcomes as well as weight.
learningObjective: Evaluate health behaviour using meaningful functional outcomes as well as weight.

title: Sustaining a new health habit
stem: A client has built a comfortable routine of short daily walks. Ice now makes the outdoor route unsafe, but a nearby indoor corridor is accessible. Which strategies support maintaining the habit? Select all that apply.
options: Use the accessible indoor route on icy days
Keep the usual daily time as an activity cue
Combine missed walks into one long weekend session
Review the adapted routine after the first week
why: A usable alternative setting preserves activity while avoiding the identified weather hazard.
A stable cue can support continuation of the established routine.
A long compensatory session may exceed current tolerance and does not maintain the established daily pattern.
Early review can identify whether the replacement route and schedule actually work.
takeaway: Anticipate barriers and backup routines when maintaining behaviour change.
learningObjective: Anticipate barriers and backup routines when maintaining behaviour change.

title: Prenatal pica disclosure
stem: A pregnant client quietly reports eating clay and persistent ice cravings. What response best addresses this disclosure?
options: Explore the substances and amounts and arrange clinical review
Discuss food alternatives for managing the cravings
Review the balance of the client's usual meals
Offer culturally relevant prenatal nutrition information
why: The specific nonfood intake warrants nutritional and exposure assessment, including possible associated deficiency.
Alternatives may be discussed, but do not establish whether ingestion or an underlying deficiency requires treatment.
General intake review is useful but should not replace assessment of the reported substances.
Culturally responsive support matters, but this disclosure also needs a specific clinical assessment.
takeaway: Assess nonfood cravings during pregnancy without judgment.
learningObjective: Assess nonfood cravings during pregnancy without judgment.

title: Fish advice during pregnancy
stem: A pregnant client stopped eating fish after hearing about mercury and wants to include it again. What guidance is most appropriate?
options: Continue avoiding fish through the pregnancy
Choose lower-mercury fish using Canadian guidance
Choose locally caught fish as the lower-mercury source
Use thorough cooking to make higher-mercury fish suitable
why: Fish can provide useful nutrients; species-specific choices can reduce exposure without broad exclusion.
Current Canadian advice helps select nutritious species and limit higher-mercury choices.
Mercury in locally caught fish depends on species and location; local advisories still matter.
Cooking does not reliably remove mercury already present in fish.
takeaway: Use species-specific guidance rather than blanket fish avoidance.
learningObjective: Use species-specific guidance rather than blanket fish avoidance.

title: Prenatal supplement duplication
stem: A pregnant client already takes a prenatal multivitamin and plans to add two products marketed for pregnancy. What product information should the nurse review first?
options: The symptoms the client hopes each product will improve
Whether each product has a Canadian licence number
The ingredients and total daily amounts across the products
The proposed times for taking each product with meals
why: Treatment goals are useful, but the products must first be checked for duplicating or unsuitable ingredients.
Licensing does not establish that combining products is appropriate for this client.
Combining products can duplicate nutrients or introduce ingredients requiring further review.
Spacing products does not prevent excessive total intake of duplicate ingredients.
takeaway: Review combined supplement ingredients before adding prenatal products.
learningObjective: Review combined supplement ingredients before adding prenatal products.

title: Persistent pregnancy vomiting
stem: A pregnant client has repeatedly vomited small sips of fluid for the past day, feels dizzy on standing and urinates much less than usual. What should the nurse advise?
options: Continue small fluid trials and review progress tomorrow
Request a routine review of the home antiemetic plan
Arrange a telephone symptom check later in the day
Obtain prompt clinical assessment for dehydration
why: Persistent inability to retain even small amounts plus reduced urine makes continued home trials insufficient.
An antiemetic review may be needed, but the current hydration findings require timely clinical assessment.
Later telephone monitoring may delay assessment of significant fluid depletion.
Poor retention, postural dizziness and reduced urine together indicate a need for prompt assessment and treatment planning.
takeaway: Escalate pregnancy vomiting when fluid tolerance and hydration worsen.
learningObjective: Escalate pregnancy vomiting when fluid tolerance and hydration worsen.

title: Preparing for prenatal appointments
stem: Before the first prenatal visit, a client started an herbal nausea product and has questions about recurrent low mood. A previous pregnancy involved gestational diabetes. Which preparations support the visit? Select all that apply.
options: Bring the labels of current medicines and supplements
Bring details of the previous pregnancy complication
Wait to discuss low mood until the nausea has settled
Write down the mood concerns and their effects on daily life
why: Actual product details help the clinician assess ingredients and pregnancy exposures.
The previous complication can influence the current assessment and monitoring plan.
Mood concerns are relevant now and need not await resolution of physical symptoms.
Specific concerns and functional effects support assessment of emotional wellbeing.
takeaway: Include treatment history, obstetric history and emotional concerns in prenatal review.
learningObjective: Include treatment history, obstetric history and emotional concerns in prenatal review.

title: Breastfeeding and return to work
stem: A breastfeeding parent returns to eight-hour shifts in a month and wants to provide expressed milk. The employer can arrange private breaks, but the parent has not tried expressing or confirmed storage access. What is most useful now?
options: Build a frozen milk supply over the next month
Practise expression and confirm workable break and storage arrangements
Move daytime feeds to the evening before returning
Ask the caregiver to introduce scheduled milk feeds now
why: A supply may help, but does not establish how milk will be expressed and stored during workdays.
Practice and actual workplace arrangements address the specific untested parts of the transition.
Changing infant feeding times does not resolve milk expression and comfort needs during work.
Caregiver feeding practice can help, but does not answer the parent's workplace expression and storage questions.
takeaway: Plan milk expression and workplace feasibility before returning to employment.
learningObjective: Plan milk expression and workplace feasibility before returning to employment.

title: A breastfeeding parent's medication question
stem: A breastfeeding parent takes a prescribed maintenance medicine and is told by a friend to stop breastfeeding. The parent and infant are well and no adverse effect is reported. What should the nurse do first?
options: Arrange a switch to another medicine in the same class
Suggest feeding immediately before each medicine dose
Obtain medicine-specific advice using parent and infant details
Recommend expressing and discarding milk until the next visit
why: An alternative may be needed for some medicines, but the actual medicine should first be assessed.
Timing may not meaningfully reduce exposure for every drug and cannot substitute for specific advice.
Drug properties, dose, infant age and clinical factors guide whether feeding or treatment changes are needed.
Routine interruption can be unnecessary and should not be advised from an unverified general claim.
takeaway: Obtain medication-specific lactation information before recommending changes.
learningObjective: Obtain medication-specific lactation information before recommending changes.

title: Gradual weaning
stem: A parent chooses to wean and asks how to reduce breast discomfort. No urgent reason requires abrupt cessation. Which general approach is best?
options: Replace feeds gradually while monitoring comfort and infant intake
Replace the breastfeeds together at the start of the week
Reduce fluid intake while reducing breastfeeds
Use firm breast binding during the transition
why: Gradual reduction gives milk production time to adjust and allows feeding adequacy and comfort to be assessed.
Abrupt replacement can cause uncomfortable fullness and may increase complications.
Fluid restriction is not a routine safe method of reducing milk production.
Firm binding can increase discomfort and does not replace gradual adjustment and assessment.
takeaway: Plan gradual weaning when circumstances allow.
learningObjective: Plan gradual weaning when circumstances allow.

title: Infant vitamin guidance
stem: A healthy two-month-old term infant is exclusively breastfed. The parent takes a routine prenatal vitamin and asks about preventing vitamin D deficiency. What should the nurse recommend?
options: Rely on the parent's routine prenatal vitamin for the infant
Use regular direct sun exposure for the infant
Begin vitamin D when complementary foods are introduced
Use the recommended infant vitamin D supplement
why: Routine maternal supplementation does not replace the standard infant supplementation recommendation.
Sun exposure is not a reliable or recommended substitute for infant supplementation.
Waiting for complementary feeding leaves the early supplementation need unaddressed.
Canadian guidance recommends vitamin D supplementation for breastfed infants; confirm the appropriate product and instructions.
takeaway: Include recommended vitamin supplementation in infant-feeding counselling.
learningObjective: Include recommended vitamin supplementation in infant-feeding counselling.

title: Infant food allergy planning
stem: A six-month-old infant shows feeding readiness. A caregiver wants to delay potentially allergenic foods because an older sibling has food allergy. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Ask about the infant's own eczema and reaction history
Arrange individualized introduction advice when risk concerns exist
Delay allergenic foods until the infant reaches two years
Teach the response to symptoms of a possible food reaction
why: The infant's own clinical history is relevant to risk-based introduction guidance.
Specific risk concerns can be addressed while supporting timely nutritional variety.
A blanket prolonged delay is not supported simply by a sibling's allergy and may unnecessarily restrict feeding.
Caregivers need to recognize possible reactions and know when urgent help is needed.
takeaway: Individualize allergenic-food introduction and teach reaction recognition.
learningObjective: Individualize allergenic-food introduction and teach reaction recognition.

title: Choosing a milk substitute
stem: A caregiver wants to replace a three-month-old infant's formula with fortified oat beverage because it costs less. What should the nurse explain?
options: Fortified plant beverages do not replace infant formula nutritionally
An unsweetened beverage provides the needed infant nutrition
Adding cereal supplies the nutrients missing from the beverage
Adult calcium fortification makes oat beverage suitable for infancy
why: Infant formula is designed for infant requirements; the nurse should also help address the cost barrier.
Absence of added sugar does not establish a suitable nutrient balance for a young infant.
Cereal does not recreate the composition or complete nutrition of infant formula.
A fortification claim for some nutrients does not establish overall nutritional adequacy for a young infant.
takeaway: Distinguish ordinary plant beverages from nutritionally appropriate infant feeds.
learningObjective: Distinguish ordinary plant beverages from nutritionally appropriate infant feeds.

title: Bottle-to-cup development
stem: An 18-month-old carries a milk bottle and sips throughout the day, then eats little at meals. Growth and swallowing assessments are reassuring. Which plan best addresses the pattern?
options: Offer smaller bottles more frequently between meals
Provide structured meals and snacks with open-cup practice
Offer the bottle before each meal to settle the toddler
Move the milk to a spill-proof cup for continued sipping
why: Frequent milk access can continue to displace appetite for food even in smaller bottles.
A predictable eating pattern and cup development reduce continuous milk grazing and support age-appropriate meals.
Milk before meals may further reduce appetite for solid food.
Changing the container while preserving continuous intake does not address the grazing pattern.
takeaway: Support cup skills and structured meals when bottles displace food.
learningObjective: Support cup skills and structured meals when bottles displace food.

title: Preventing prolonged sugar exposure
stem: A school-age child sips a sweet drink throughout the afternoon. Which change best targets dental risk?
options: Keep the drink but change the cup
Add a straw while maintaining continuous sipping
Choose water between meals and limit prolonged sugary sipping
Brush the child's teeth after the afternoon drink period
why: Cup type alone does not remove sugar exposure.
A straw does not eliminate repeated sugar contact.
Water reduces repeated exposure that promotes decay.
Brushing remains important, but reducing repeated sugary exposure directly addresses the pattern described.
takeaway: Reduce the frequency and duration of sugary drink exposure.
learningObjective: Reduce the frequency and duration of sugary drink exposure.

title: Children's primary teeth
stem: A caregiver asks whether treating decay in a primary tooth matters because it will fall out. What is the best explanation?
options: Treatment matters only if the tooth is visible
A primary tooth cannot affect eating comfort
Decay is harmless until the permanent tooth appears
Primary teeth support eating, speech and space for permanent teeth
why: Tooth function and infection risk matter beyond appearance.
Decay can cause pain and impair chewing.
Untreated decay can cause problems before permanent eruption.
Preserving primary tooth health supports several developmental functions.
takeaway: Explain why primary teeth need treatment and preventive care.
learningObjective: Explain why primary teeth need treatment and preventive care.

title: Supporting infant motor exploration
stem: A four-month-old has few opportunities to move freely on the floor. Which proposed activities add active movement practice while awake? Select all that apply.
options: Place safe toys within reach during supervised floor play
Offer brief supervised tummy-time periods as tolerated
Show a musical video while the infant sits in a supportive seat
Respond to the infant while encouraging reaching during play
why: Reaching from a safe floor position gives the infant opportunities to practise movement.
Short supported opportunities for awake prone movement help build strength and control.
Seat-based viewing does not provide the same opportunity to practise floor movement.
Responsive interaction paired with reaching supports movement practice and social engagement.
takeaway: Offer safe awake movement and responsive interaction.
learningObjective: Offer safe awake movement and responsive interaction.

title: Recognizing play readiness
stem: During teaching, an infant repeatedly turns away, yawns and fusses after several minutes of stimulation. What should the nurse suggest?
options: Increase sound and movement to regain attention
Pause stimulation and allow a calming break
Continue until the infant smiles again
Change toys rapidly without stopping the session
why: Additional stimulation may intensify overload.
Disengagement cues can indicate a need for rest or reduced input.
Continuing despite cues does not respect the infant's regulation needs.
Rapid changes still maintain stimulation when a break is indicated.
takeaway: Respond to infant disengagement cues during play.
learningObjective: Respond to infant disengagement cues during play.

title: Toddler tantrums in public
stem: A caregiver reports tantrums when a tired toddler must leave the park. Which anticipatory strategy is most appropriate?
options: Negotiate a different departure time after every tantrum
Explain long-term consequences during peak crying
Plan around fatigue and give a brief predictable transition warning
Avoid all outings until tantrums stop
why: Inconsistent limits can make transitions less predictable.
Peak distress limits the toddler's ability to process complex explanation.
Planning and simple warnings address the identified trigger.
Avoidance limits family activity without building transition skills.
takeaway: Use predictable transitions and fatigue awareness to reduce toddler distress.
learningObjective: Use predictable transitions and fatigue awareness to reduce toddler distress.

title: Preparing for a new sibling
stem: A preschooler becomes clingy after a baby arrives and asks whether the parent still has time for them. Which response most directly addresses this concern?
options: Keep familiar routines and arrange regular individual time together
Give the child more responsibilities during baby care
Introduce new activities the child can complete independently
Praise the child whenever they behave like an older sibling
why: Predictable attention and continuity respond directly to the expressed concern about connection.
Involvement may help, but additional responsibility does not replace individual attention.
Independent activities can be enjoyable, but do not directly reassure the child about shared time.
Praise can support adjustment, but should not make attention depend on appearing mature.
takeaway: Support sibling adjustment with routine and individual connection.
learningObjective: Support sibling adjustment with routine and individual connection.

title: School-age body privacy
stem: A child entering school asks, "Why do I need to take off my shirt for the checkup?" What should the nurse do first?
options: Demonstrate the examination equipment on the caregiver
Ask the caregiver to explain the examination to the child
Finish discussing the history with the caregiver
Explain the examination step and how privacy will be protected
why: A demonstration may help later but does not first answer the child's question about clothing and privacy.
The caregiver may support the child, but the nurse can address the child directly in understandable language.
Deferring the question may increase uncertainty about what is about to happen.
A simple explanation, privacy protection and invitation to ask or pause support developmentally appropriate participation.
takeaway: Explain examination purpose and privacy directly to children.
learningObjective: Explain examination purpose and privacy directly to children.

title: School health planning
stem: A school-age child with well-controlled asthma is joining school sports. Which preparations support participation? Select all that apply.
options: Share the individualized asthma plan with appropriate staff and consent
Clarify symptoms and steps that require adult or urgent help
Arrange a seated scorekeeping role for each physical-education class
Practise how the child will ask an adult for assistance
why: An accessible individualized plan helps school staff provide the agreed support.
Clear escalation instructions prepare staff and child to respond if symptoms occur.
A routine nonparticipating role is not indicated solely by well-controlled asthma; activity needs should be individualized.
Age-appropriate help-seeking strengthens participation and safety.
takeaway: Coordinate school participation with individualized support and escalation plans.
learningObjective: Coordinate school participation with individualized support and escalation plans.

title: Persistent childhood snoring
stem: A parent reports nightly loud snoring, restless sleep and new daytime behaviour difficulties in a child. Which recommendation is most appropriate?
options: Arrange a clinical assessment of sleep and breathing
Keep a sleep diary until the next routine annual visit
Introduce an earlier bedtime and review behaviour next month
Change bedding to reduce possible environmental allergens
why: The combined nocturnal and daytime pattern warrants assessment for sleep-disordered breathing and other causes.
A diary may contribute useful information, but delaying assessment leaves the concerning pattern unevaluated.
Sleep routines matter, but do not assess a possible breathing-related disturbance.
Allergen review may be relevant, but should not replace assessment of the full symptom pattern.
takeaway: Assess persistent snoring with disrupted sleep or daytime effects.
learningObjective: Assess persistent snoring with disrupted sleep or daytime effects.

title: A sports concussion return question
stem: A student with a diagnosed concussion has begun light activity under a return plan. Symptoms are improving and the student wants to join a contact game today. What should the nurse reinforce?
options: Full play is reasonable once symptoms feel better at rest
Progress through the return plan and obtain required clearance
A team noncontact practice can be used to test readiness today
Resume contact play once the missed school assignments are finished
why: Improvement at rest does not establish readiness for head-impact risk.
Staged progression and medical clearance for higher-risk stages protect recovery; timing is individualized.
Team practice may carry risk and should match the prescribed stage and clearance requirements, rather than serve as an unscheduled test.
Schoolwork completion alone does not establish physical readiness for contact sport.
takeaway: Reinforce a graduated assessed return after concussion.
learningObjective: Reinforce a graduated assessed return after concussion.

title: Adolescent health goal ownership
stem: A parent requests a diet plan for a teenager who has not yet discussed goals with staff. No urgent nutritional problem has been identified. What should the nurse do first?
options: Review the parent's proposed menu for nutritional balance
Arrange a joint family nutrition teaching session
Invite the teenager to discuss their own priorities and concerns
Record baseline body measurements for the proposed plan
why: Menu review may help after understanding the adolescent's needs and perspective.
Family teaching can be useful, but the teenager should first have a meaningful opportunity to express goals.
A developmentally appropriate discussion establishes the adolescent's perspective before adopting another person's plan.
Measurements do not establish the purpose, relevance or adolescent participation in the proposed change.
takeaway: Include adolescents in defining their own health-promotion goals.
learningObjective: Include adolescents in defining their own health-promotion goals.

title: Preparing for first menstruation
stem: A preadolescent understands the basic explanation of menstruation but worries it may start during class. What teaching best addresses the immediate concern?
options: Review how cycle lengths can vary during adolescence
Explain the reproductive organs using a labelled diagram
Discuss comfort measures for possible menstrual cramps
Plan accessible supplies and a trusted school contact
why: Cycle information is useful but does not provide a response to an unexpected start at school.
The learner already understands the basic process and is asking about practical readiness.
Symptom relief may be discussed, but the immediate concern is managing the first bleeding during class.
Concrete supplies and a person to approach make the expected developmental event more manageable.
takeaway: Pair puberty information with a practical preparedness plan.
learningObjective: Pair puberty information with a practical preparedness plan.

title: Adolescent online health information
stem: A teenager sees an influencer promoting a supplement to improve concentration. Which actions help evaluate the claim? Select all that apply.
options: Check the creator's relevant qualifications
Examine the supporting evidence and when it was updated
Treat the number of likes as evidence of effectiveness
Check whether the creator profits from product sales
why: Relevant expertise helps assess credibility, though it does not by itself prove the claim.
Evidence and currency help distinguish a supported recommendation from a promotional assertion.
Popularity does not demonstrate a clinical benefit or safety.
A financial interest may influence how benefits and limitations are presented.
takeaway: Assess expertise, evidence and commercial influence in online health advice.
learningObjective: Assess expertise, evidence and commercial influence in online health advice.

title: Sexual consent education
stem: During health teaching, a young adult asks whether agreement on a previous occasion means consent today. What is the best explanation?
options: Consent is ongoing and must apply to the current activity
A previous relationship establishes continuing consent
Lack of an objection always establishes consent
Consent is needed only when contraception is not used
why: A prior agreement does not replace voluntary current agreement.
Relationship status does not establish consent for every activity.
Silence or inability to respond does not reliably establish consent.
Consent is separate from contraceptive use.
takeaway: Teach consent as voluntary, specific and ongoing.
learningObjective: Teach consent as voluntary, specific and ongoing.

title: New pain with sexual activity
stem: Eight weeks after birth, a client reports repeated pain during intercourse and worries that a repaired tear has not healed. They have no fever or heavy bleeding. What should the nurse do first?
options: Suggest a lubricant for the next attempt at intercourse
Offer a private assessment of symptoms and healing
Book the concern for the next annual examination
Refer directly for a pelvic-floor exercise program
why: Lubricant may help some causes, but the reported healing concern needs assessment before assuming dryness.
A private review can distinguish healing, tissue, muscle and other contributors and guide appropriate support.
Persistent pain deserves timely review rather than an automatic lengthy delay.
Pelvic-floor support may be useful after assessing the nature of the discomfort.
takeaway: Invite assessment of postpartum sexual discomfort without assumptions.
learningObjective: Invite assessment of postpartum sexual discomfort without assumptions.

title: Menopause and pregnancy prevention
stem: A 47-year-old who uses condoms has irregular periods and new hot flashes. They do not want pregnancy and ask whether they can stop contraception. What should the nurse recommend?
options: Use cycle tracking as the pregnancy-prevention method
Wait for another menstrual period before using condoms again
Continue pregnancy prevention while reviewing the clinical history
Request one hormone test to decide whether contraception can stop
why: Irregular cycles make prediction difficult and do not establish that pregnancy cannot occur.
Pregnancy can occur before another period confirms continuing ovulation.
Perimenopausal symptoms do not establish loss of fertility; current guidance and individual history should guide stopping.
A single hormone value can fluctuate and does not by itself establish the appropriate stopping point.
takeaway: Do not equate early menopausal symptoms with established infertility.
learningObjective: Do not equate early menopausal symptoms with established infertility.

title: A new changing skin lesion
stem: A client shows photographs of a mole that has become more asymmetric and changed colour over six weeks. It is painless. What should the nurse recommend?
options: Continue photographs until the next annual skin review
Begin a monthly self-check for new itching
Watch for bleeding before arranging a skin appointment
Arrange clinical assessment of the changing lesion
why: Photographs document evolution but do not replace assessment of changes already present.
Itching is not required for a changing lesion to warrant review.
Waiting for bleeding can postpone assessment of concerning evolution.
The documented change warrants clinical evaluation despite the absence of pain.
takeaway: Refer evolving skin lesions rather than waiting for discomfort.
learningObjective: Refer evolving skin lesions rather than waiting for discomfort.

title: Oral health with dry mouth
stem: An older adult has persistent dry mouth after a medication change and reports difficulty eating dry foods. Which approaches are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Review possible medication effects with the prescriber or pharmacist
Arrange dental guidance and oral-health prevention
Use frequent sugar-containing lozenges for continuing relief
Assess fluid intake and associated oral symptoms
why: A review can identify modifiable contributors while preserving needed treatment.
Reduced saliva can affect comfort and dental health, so prevention and assessment are useful.
Frequent sugar exposure can increase dental caries risk in an already dry mouth.
Hydration and other symptoms help identify additional causes and the effect on intake.
takeaway: Assess persistent dry mouth and protect oral health while reviewing causes.
learningObjective: Assess persistent dry mouth and protect oral health while reviewing causes.

title: Sun protection with a new medicine
stem: A client starting a prescribed medication with a photosensitivity warning gardens daily. Which plan best reduces exposure while preserving the activity?
options: Use protective clothing and garden during lower-exposure periods
Change to higher-SPF sunscreen for the usual midday session
Take the medicine at bedtime before the next gardening day
Move the garden chair into light tree shade at midday
why: Covering skin and adjusting timing address exposure while retaining the valued activity and prescribed treatment.
Sunscreen helps, but changing SPF alone does not address duration, timing or exposed skin.
Night-time dosing does not necessarily remove the medicine's photosensitizing effect during the day.
Shade can reduce exposure but does not eliminate ultraviolet radiation or the value of other protection.
takeaway: Adapt outdoor routines when medication increases sun sensitivity.
learningObjective: Adapt outdoor routines when medication increases sun sensitivity.

title: Financial strain and nutrition priorities
stem: A client eats ordinary foods comfortably and has no prescribed supplement need. Their remaining food budget could buy a marketed nutrition powder or several days of groceries. What is most useful now?
options: Suggest a trial of the powder at the labelled dose
Plan affordable meals using the available grocery budget
Arrange a routine nutrition referral for next month
Compare the powder's nutrient panel with a standard meal
why: The product has no established individualized indication and may displace the available food budget.
A feasible food plan directly supports the immediate need while further resource support can be explored.
A later review may help but does not address food needs over the next several days.
Product comparison may be informative, but a practical ordinary-food plan directly addresses the immediate budget decision for a client able to eat.
takeaway: Prioritize adequate feasible food access over unassessed commercial products.
learningObjective: Prioritize adequate feasible food access over unassessed commercial products.

title: Movement with a wheelchair
stem: A wheelchair user wants better cardiovascular fitness but develops shoulder pain after five minutes of self-propulsion. An accessible exercise service is available. What should the nurse recommend first?
options: Increase wheelchair-pushing time by five minutes each day
Begin a daily arm-ergometer session at the community gym
Request rehabilitation assessment for an adapted activity plan
Substitute a daily wheelchair sprint for the current routine
why: Increasing load despite pain may aggravate a limitation that has not been assessed.
Arm exercise may be useful, but current shoulder symptoms should inform the chosen modality and intensity.
Assessment can identify a suitable accessible option while accounting for shoulder pain and current endurance.
Higher-intensity propulsion increases shoulder demand and does not address the reported limitation.
takeaway: Make physical-activity plans accessible to current mobility.
learningObjective: Make physical-activity plans accessible to current mobility.

title: Peer education and misinformation
stem: During a class, a participant says they will replace their prescribed treatment with a supplement promoted as a cure. Several others begin writing down the product name. What should the nurse do next?
options: Arrange a private conversation with the participant after class
Ask everyone to review the product website at home
Send the group an evidence resource after the session
Clarify the claim respectfully with the group now
why: Private follow-up may help, but the shared claim is already influencing other participants.
Directing learners to promotional material can reinforce an unexamined claim.
A later resource leaves the immediate potentially consequential misunderstanding unaddressed.
Timely respectful clarification protects learning while avoiding humiliation; individual treatment changes still need appropriate clinical review.
takeaway: Correct health misinformation while preserving participation and respect.
learningObjective: Correct health misinformation while preserving participation and respect.

title: Assessing health-program reach
stem: A free clinic attracts mostly people who already use preventive services. Which changes may improve reach to underserved clients? Select all that apply.
options: Ask nonattenders about access barriers
Partner with trusted local organizations
Survey current attendees about appointment convenience
Adapt location or hours based on community feedback
why: Nonattender perspectives reveal barriers current users may not face.
Trusted partnerships can improve relevance and access.
Current attendees may not face the barriers that prevent others from using the clinic; their responses alone do not represent the unreached group.
Practical adaptation can address barriers identified by intended users.
takeaway: Evaluate who is missing from a program as well as who attends.
learningObjective: Evaluate who is missing from a program as well as who attends.

title: Newborn jaundice and feeding
stem: During a home visit, a four-day-old newborn is increasingly yellow and unusually difficult to wake for feeds. What is the nurse's priority?
options: Arrange urgent clinical assessment of the newborn
Schedule an additional feeding-support visit tomorrow
Repeat the weight at the next routine home visit
Arrange a routine outpatient bilirubin appointment later in the week
why: Jaundice with abnormal sleepiness and poor feeding can indicate significant illness or bilirubin elevation and requires urgent assessment.
Feeding support is important, but tomorrow's visit would delay assessment of current abnormal alertness.
A weight trend can inform care but is insufficient for this concerning current presentation.
The infant's clinical condition needs urgent review rather than delayed laboratory scheduling.
takeaway: Escalate newborn jaundice associated with poor feeding or unusual sleepiness.
learningObjective: Escalate newborn jaundice associated with poor feeding or unusual sleepiness.

title: Postpartum infection warning
stem: On day five after birth, a client reports a temperature of 38.6°C, increasing pelvic pain and foul-smelling discharge. What should the nurse advise?
