options: Review perineal hygiene at the next home visit
Obtain prompt clinical assessment today
Recheck temperature after an antipyretic before deciding
Discuss the discharge at the scheduled postpartum review
why: Hygiene advice does not evaluate a possible postpartum infection.
Fever with increasing pelvic pain and abnormal odour requires prompt assessment for infection and treatment.
A lower temperature after medication would not resolve the infection concern raised by the combined findings.
Routine review is too delayed for the current symptom pattern.
takeaway: Teach prompt assessment for postpartum fever with worsening pain or abnormal discharge.
learningObjective: Teach prompt assessment for postpartum fever with worsening pain or abnormal discharge.

title: Postpartum thrombosis-prevention planning
stem: After an uncomplicated birth, a client prefers staying in bed most of the day despite being cleared for mobilization. Which teaching best supports thrombosis prevention?
options: Resume regular gentle movement according to the recovery plan
Delay routine walking until postpartum bleeding has ended
Substitute seated ankle movements for all permitted walking
Use compression stockings as the entire prevention plan
why: Appropriate mobilization reduces prolonged immobility while respecting recovery.
Expected postpartum bleeding alone does not justify prolonged inactivity after clearance to mobilize.
Ankle exercises may complement care but need not replace tolerated permitted movement.
Mechanical measures, when indicated, complement rather than automatically replace an individualized activity plan.
takeaway: Encourage appropriate postpartum mobility within the individual recovery plan.
learningObjective: Encourage appropriate postpartum mobility within the individual recovery plan.

title: Postpartum bleeding change
stem: A client one week after birth reports suddenly much heavier vaginal bleeding and feels faint while sitting. Which advice takes priority?
options: Call the routine postpartum line and leave a message
Ask a relative to drive to the usual clinic
Rest, drink fluids and measure the next pad
Call emergency services for immediate help
why: A routine callback can delay assessment of possible circulatory compromise.
Family transport to a routine clinic may not provide timely emergency support if the client deteriorates.
Rest can be appropriate while help is coming, but fluids and pad counting do not replace emergency evaluation.
Heavy bleeding with faintness raises concern for significant blood loss requiring emergency assessment and treatment.
takeaway: Treat heavy postpartum bleeding with faintness as an emergency.
learningObjective: Treat heavy postpartum bleeding with faintness as an emergency.

title: Parent learning after discharge
stem: Parents are reviewing when to seek help for their newborn. Which observations need prompt clinical attention? Select all that apply.
options: Unusual difficulty waking enough to complete feeds
Brief hiccups after a feed with comfortable breathing
Persistent chest retractions with difficulty feeding
Occasional sneezing while feeding and activity remain usual
A marked feeding reduction accompanied by fewer wet diapers
why: Abnormal alertness and poor feeding can signal illness or inadequate intake and need prompt assessment.
Brief uncomplicated hiccups are common and do not by themselves indicate urgent illness.
Persistent respiratory distress requires immediate emergency assessment rather than a routine callback.
Isolated sneezing with otherwise normal function does not carry the same urgency as respiratory distress or reduced intake.
A sustained change in feeding and urine output raises concern for inadequate intake or illness.
takeaway: Include feeding, alertness and breathing warning signs in newborn teaching.
learningObjective: Include feeding, alertness and breathing warning signs in newborn teaching.

title: Childhood fever learning focus
stem: A caregiver asks why a child with a lower temperature might need help sooner than one with a higher fever. Which example best demonstrates this?
options: A toddler at 38.1°C is breathing with marked effort
A preschooler at 39.0°C is drinking and playing
A school-age child at 38.5°C asks for a drink
A toddler at 38.8°C settles comfortably with a parent
why: Significant breathing difficulty requires urgent assessment regardless of the modest temperature reading.
The fever still needs monitoring, but normal intake and activity are reassuring compared with respiratory distress.
Requesting and taking fluids is a useful reassuring sign in the absence of other concerning findings.
Comfort and responsiveness matter alongside temperature; this description lacks the urgent breathing cue.
takeaway: Teach assessment of the whole child rather than temperature alone.
learningObjective: Teach assessment of the whole child rather than temperature alone.

title: Preparing a child's hospital visit
stem: A school-age child asks whether a planned blood test will hurt. Which response best prepares the child?
options: Let me show you the equipment before we discuss sensations
You may feel a brief pinch; we can practise your coping plan
Ask your caregiver what happened during their blood test
Look at this game while I get everything ready
why: Equipment demonstration can help but should not postpone answering the direct concern.
An honest concise description paired with agreed coping support provides realistic preparation.
A caregiver's experience may differ and does not replace the nurse's direct explanation to the child.
Distraction can be useful, but preparation should also answer the child's question honestly.
takeaway: Give honest age-appropriate information about expected procedural sensations.
learningObjective: Give honest age-appropriate information about expected procedural sensations.

title: A new caregiving arrangement
stem: A grandparent who will care for an infant plans to use a pillow for sleep; the parents were taught to keep the sleep space clear. The family wants the grandparent involved. What is most useful?
options: Give the parents another copy of the safe-sleep leaflet
Ask the parents to relay the updated advice tonight
Review the sleep setup together and check caregiver understanding
Arrange a separate teaching visit after care has started
why: Another copy for the parents does not establish the grandparent's understanding.
Relayed information can help but may leave the specific difference unresolved.
Shared practical review directly addresses the conflicting plan and supports a consistent routine.
Waiting until care begins leaves the known setup issue unresolved for the first sleep.
takeaway: Update and coordinate health teaching across the infant's caregivers.
learningObjective: Update and coordinate health teaching across the infant's caregivers.

title: Choosing developmentally useful toys
stem: A four-month-old turns toward a parent's voice and reaches for a simple rattle. The parent wonders whether an expensive electronic activity centre is necessary for development. Which activity best builds on the infant's cues?
options: Use recorded speech from a toy during independent play
Provide a new electronic sequence at each play period
Use the activity centre for the main daily play session
Respond to sounds and take turns exploring the safe rattle
why: Recorded speech does not adapt to this infant's signals like responsive interaction.
Novelty alone does not establish a better developmental experience.
An activity centre may be one option, but is not necessary to support the observed interest and interaction.
Responsive turn-taking and safe exploration build on the infant's current social and motor behaviours.
takeaway: Emphasize responsive play over costly developmental marketing.
learningObjective: Emphasize responsive play over costly developmental marketing.

title: Evaluating a prevention plan over time
stem: A client met a regular-meal goal but is moving to evening shifts. The new workplace provides a refrigerator and a scheduled meal break. Which adaptations are useful? Select all that apply.
options: Review meal times and foods that fit the new break
Prepare meals that can be stored safely at work
Keep the previous meal times for the first month
Arrange a follow-up to review the new routine
why: Planning around actual break availability makes the goal feasible in the changed schedule.
Available storage can support a practical meal strategy matched to the workplace.
The previous timing may conflict with the new shift and undermine a previously achievable goal.
Early review allows the client and nurse to evaluate and refine the adaptation.
takeaway: Reassess and adapt health-promotion plans when circumstances change.
learningObjective: Reassess and adapt health-promotion plans when circumstances change.
